title: Sell Mineral Rights in Jeannette, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Jeannette, PA
metaDescription: Jeannette, PA's Glass City history left behind fractured mineral estates. See what your interest is worth in today's Westmoreland Marcellus market.
heroLead: Jeannette earned the nickname Glass City for its glassworks, but the ground under those old factories and the farms around them still carries valuable Marcellus mineral rights.
intro: When the glass factories were running full shifts, nobody in Jeannette was thinking about what sat two miles beneath their feet. The farms that used to ring the city got sold off in pieces as the town grew, and a lot of those old sale deeds reserved oil, gas, and mineral rights for the seller — meaning the family who once farmed that land may still own the minerals under a Jeannette subdivision today, even though they haven't lived there in three generations.

sections.heading: Tracing Ownership Back Past the Subdivision
paragraphs: Because Jeannette grew outward from farmland into residential blocks, mineral ownership here often doesn't match surface ownership at all. We start every Jeannette file by pulling the original farm-to-lot conveyance to see whether minerals were reserved, and if so, who they passed to. That single document usually explains why a family with no connection to a current Jeannette address still gets an occasional letter about a gas lease.

sections.heading: Westmoreland's Wet-Gas Advantage
paragraphs: Jeannette sits well inside the wet-gas window of the Marcellus, the same window that runs through Hempfield and Sewickley Townships. Wet gas carries natural gas liquids that get separated and sold at a processing plant, which is part of why operators have kept coming back to this stretch of Westmoreland even during years when Appalachian dry-gas prices were weak.

sections.heading: What a Fair Look at Your Interest Involves
paragraphs: We don't quote a number without seeing the deed, the unit filing if one exists, and any royalty history tied to the parcel. Values here depend heavily on whether your acreage sits inside an active or planned unit, so a fair offer has to be tied to what's actually happening on the ground around you, not a flat per-acre figure pulled from a website.

faqs.question: My family moved away from Jeannette generations ago — do we still own minerals there?
faqs.answer: Possibly. If an ancestor sold the surface but reserved minerals, that reservation still runs with the land today, and the Westmoreland County Recorder's office in Greensburg will have the record.

faqs.question: Does it matter that the land above is now residential?
faqs.answer: Not for ownership — reserved mineral rights survive subdivision and residential development. It can affect drilling access, but not your ownership.

faqs.question: How do I find out if a unit already covers my parcel?
faqs.answer: Unit declarations are filed at the county recorder's office and are public. We check this as a first step on every Jeannette inquiry.
